new_statements.quote: Pasch (1983:207) considers CS (3b) and (3b') as one (see also the WP 'maize' isogloss map in Lisimba [1982:381]), even though the first vowel and the tone pattern are different. In Kwamashi, for instance, the underlying scheme of mùndárè does not reflect *HH, but *LH, e.g. *-pʊ̀ká 'insect' > thìpúkà, *-cʊ̀kɪ́ 'hair' > dìhúkì.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand phonological information opened: Kwamashi words carry lexical H/L tone with regular reflexes of Proto-Bantu tone patterns (all Kwamashi forms in the paper are tone-marked). No statement anywhere about word stress or accent placement. The only stress remark covering the area is Kashoki & Mann 1978:70, an areal generalisation that Zambian Bantu languages have 'more or less evenly stressed' syllables, non-distinctive stress and syllabic H/L tone -- not made for Mashi by name.
new_statements.domain_note: Implicit evidence only (tone-marked citation forms from field notes); not a prosodic description. A dedicated description (Lisimba 1982, Luyana dialectology incl. Mashi/Kwandu) exists but could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Target is Mashi of Zambia/Angola/Namibia (Kwamashi, Bantu K34, iso mho; dialects Mashi, North Kwandu, South Kwandu; Bostoen's data are from Kwamashi speakers at Shangombo/Sioma). It must not be confused with Mashi = Shi of DR Congo (iso shr, Glottolog shii1238, Bantu JD53): two of Glottolog's refs attached to mash1267 (Muhasha 1996 'Time expression in Mashi', Revue africaine de communications sociales; the White Fathers' Dictionnaire français-mashi / Vocabulaire shi-français) concern the Congolese language. Kashoki & Mann 1978's stress remark is areal ('Zambian languages'), not about Mashi.

sources.locator: p. 22 (section 2.3 'maize'); data from Bostoen's Kwamashi field notes, Shangombo/Sioma 2005 (p. 16)
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. First-hand Kwamashi (K34) field data (Bostoen FN 2005, Shangombo/Sioma) are fully tone-marked and p.22 states Kwamashi forms show regular Proto-Bantu tone reflexes (*LH > thìpúkà, dìhúkì), i.e. lexical tone; no prosodic statement beyond that.

sources.note: No typology field; dialects North Kwandu, South Kwandu, Mashi; Latin script developed 2011; Bible portions 2013.

sources.citation: Kashoki, Mubanga E. & Michael Mann. 1978. A general sketch of the Bantu languages of Zambia. In S. Ohannessian & M. E. Kashoki (eds), Language in Zambia, 47-100. London: International African Institute.
sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'Tone and Stress' p.70 is an AREAL statement for 'Zambian languages': 'syllables are more or less evenly stressed... stress in Zambian languages does not distinguish words from each other in meaning'; every syllable carries tone (H vs L). Mashi and N. Kwandu appear only in the Fortune 1963 lexicostatistic table (Table 2:5, p.59) and Kwandu is named for dental fricatives (p.68); no Mashi-specific prosodic statement.
